messages.author: df1e8c4ee64c5304
messages.subject: Is it better to invoke STAN with no defined set of inits?
parts:
Another STAN newbie question.
I was looking at the documentation for the parameter list for STAN and finally read the init information carefully.  In BUGS you have to supply your inits, and for better or for worse, many times the inits for all of the chains are the same.  But one should really want a variety of (credible) inits to be sure that one is not finding only a local maximum.  I saw that with STAN, if the init is not defined, the default is "random," defined as "randomly generated by STAN," presumably on "the unconstrained support." 
This sounds exactly like what one would want to use as differing inits for multiple chains.  Does this imply that, barring a special situation, one would do better to invoke STAN without a specified init?  Sounds pretty neat to me.
Larry Hunsicker

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it better to invoke STAN with no defined set of inits?
parts:
Yes. Because we can map unconstrained params back to constrained,
we can do init uniformly on (-2,2) on the unconstrained scale for
each chain and then map back to constrained. The description of how
all those transforms work is a chapter in the manual.

If models are really complex, it can help to give it inits.

I believe BUGS will do automatic inits for you, as will JAGS, but
JAGS does them the same deterministic way for each chain --- I don't
know what BUGS does.

- Bob

The downside is that this approach is that it assumes roughly equal scales of all variables, but this is anyway a recommended way of writing models...

On Jun 21, 2015, at 4:15 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I see. Would it be possible to, let's say, run the optimizer on a model for a limited number of iteration steps, then add some random noise to the result and use that?

Yes. You want the noise for diffuse inits? Because you've
probably already lost the ability to detect multimodality unless
the whole operation of optimization plus sampling gets replicated
from differing optimization inits.

I'm hoping that the variational inference will be better for
inits like this --- it won't get tripped up by models with no posterior
mode (hence no MLE), like most clustering or hierarchical models.
> To make this happen from the interfaces is control over the iteration steps in the optimizers,

What kind of control are you looking for? You can set the max
number of steps externally.
> but certainly this is better done internally inside Stan as it can more easily operate on the unconstrained scale.

You mean avoiding the roundtrip of constraining for the answer
of optimization and then unconstraining to form the init in Stan?
I think that cost will be negligible compared to everything else and
will also be something we want to inspect on the constrained scale.
> Maybe this is worth a ticket to track for the future?

If you have a concrete behavior to suggest, it should be
a feature request issue. If it's a more general line of inquiry
that requires more research, it should go in our wiki of future
to-do items (I can give you editing permission if you don't have it).
> The downside is that this approach is that it assumes roughly equal scales of all variables, but this is anyway a recommended way of writing models...

What assumes equal scales?

- Bob

Andrew --- do you have any general guidelines
on starting points? I see lots of examples around where people
use some kind of rough point estimate to intialize.

Our uniform(-2,2) unconstrained was just pulled out of
thin air, though if you started at the mean of a unit
normal, it'd give you a uniform draw from the marginal 95%
interval.

But correlation and dimensionality will kill you quickly.
A multivariate normal with high correlation means that
marginal uniform(-2,2) thing puts you way out in the tails.

If you knew what the posterior was, would it matter where
you started in the typical set?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it better to invoke STAN with no defined set of inits?
parts:
I believe the original Gelman-Rubin (1992) paper on R-hat suggests a heuristic which is similar in spirit to what Sebastian describes. That is, you find “all” of the local optima using something such as EM, then build a mixture of t-distributions where each is centered at the local optima and whose variance is given by an approximation of the inverse Fisher information evaluated at that point. To run M chains, you sample N>M points from the mixture of t’s, and then apply sequential importance resampling to refine the N points to get M of them.

This was in fact a point Don was interested in hearing more about, because I recall Andrew mentioned something about this no longer being necessary when I was presenting the paper in Don’s missing data seminar. My guess is that the problem is the time it takes to find “all” of the local optima.

Slightly related: there is also work by Chuanhai Liu and Don (1996, 2002) on Markov normal-based analysis in order to define “restarting distributions”, which propose a better distribution to restart one’s chains as they run. It’s also computationally efficient because it’s just MLE on normal approximations.

Dustin

parts:
Let’s all step back and review the basics. We want to compute expectations
with respect to the posterior, which means finding neighborhoods in parameter space
which dominate the contribution to the respective integrals. We colloquially call
these neighborhoods components of the “typical set”. Markov Chain Monte Carlo
is essentially a method for discovering (convergence) and then exploring (mixing)
the typical set of a complicated posterior distribution.

Convergence to a component of the typical set is made difficult when the tails of
the posterior of pathological. For example, the posterior density can be expensive
to compute (a la stiff ODEs) or the tails can be so heavy that the chains simply
don’t have enough information to find the typical set in any finite time (a la Cauchy
tails). The immediate solution is to not start in the tails, which amounts to starting
in the typical set which is exactly what we do not know how to do.

What about trying to seed from a mode? Well modes are tricky because of the
parameterization dependence — in some parameterizations they can be closer
to the typical set than in others — but in general there’s no guarantee they offer
better initial conditions. In fact, a good Markov chain will find the typical set in about
the same time that the optimizer will find a mode — subject to the usual regularity
conditions (which we need for finite-time MCMC estimators anyways) the convergence
time is on the order of the mixing time. This ignores parameter-dependent transition
costs (i.e. ODEs becoming stiff in the tails), but those costs affect optimization just
as much as they affect the chains.

Our adaptation can mess up this intuition a bit, but that’s why I included an initial
convergence window in the adaptation — we converge for a few iterations with a
unit metric before beginning to learn a diagonal/dense one. If there are serious
convergence issues it may very well be prescient to increase the size of this
initial window.

To summarize, convergence shouldn’t take much longer than optimization. Similarly,
any “restarting distribution” will be fundamentally limited because by the time you’ve
constructed a good one you already have enough information to construct your MCMC
estimators. For example, if you want to initialize with EM then what initial conditions
do you choose for the EM algorithm? You’re not solving the problem, just sweeping
it under the rug of another step. Moreover, a good initialization or restarting distribution
won’t be all that helpful for multimodal posteriors given that finding all of the modes
will be incredibly difficult and even if you could find them all then you still have to be
able to weight them appropriately in order to construct a valid MCMC transition
(which means computing local evidences which means you need more than a
simple Markov chain).

parts:
Thanks. I'm embarassed to say I've never read the original papers.

The problem is that we have so many models that don't have
local optima. I think that's why Sebastian was suggesting "early
stopping" as it's known in the machine learning world (a procedural
approximation of a kind of regularization). That is, stop before
convergence to avoid params getting extreme values.

Assuming we approximate the Fisher info matrix somehow (say by
a smoothed Hessian as in Betancourt's SoftAbs metric), then we
still have the problem of O(N^2) entries for N dimensions, which
quickly becomes problematic for problems with thousands of parameters.

But the problem for me is that I don't see how to deal with correlation
without doing something like this.

Low rank approximations, perhaps? It's something we have to think about
for Riemannian HMC, too --- whether we can get somethin in between a diagonal
and dense metric that's more useful than diagonal but easier to compute
than the dense metric.

- Bob

Better to have init’d and lost than to never have init’d at all.

More seriously, I think we can often get reasonable starting points based on priors. This is something we should think more about when we do the graphical-models wrapper.

> On Jun 22, 2015, at 3:34 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Let’s all step back and review the basics. We want to compute expectations
> with respect to the posterior, which means finding neighborhoods in parameter space
> which dominate the contribution to the respective integrals. We colloquially call
> these neighborhoods components of the “typical set”. Markov Chain Monte Carlo
> is essentially a method for discovering (convergence) and then exploring (mixing)
> the typical set of a complicated posterior distribution.
>
> Convergence to a component of the typical set is made difficult when the tails of
> the posterior of pathological. For example, the posterior density can be expensive
> to compute (a la stiff ODEs) or the tails can be so heavy that the chains simply
> don’t have enough information to find the typical set in any finite time (a la Cauchy
> tails). The immediate solution is to not start in the tails, which amounts to starting
> in the typical set which is exactly what we do not know how to do.
>
> What about trying to seed from a mode? Well modes are tricky because of the
> parameterization dependence — in some parameterizations they can be closer
> to the typical set than in others — but in general there’s no guarantee they offer
> better initial conditions. In fact, a good Markov chain will find the typical set in about
> the same time that the optimizer will find a mode — subject to the usual regularity
> conditions (which we need for finite-time MCMC estimators anyways) the convergence
> time is on the order of the mixing time. This ignores parameter-dependent transition
> costs (i.e. ODEs becoming stiff in the tails), but those costs affect optimization just
> as much as they affect the chains.
>
> Our adaptation can mess up this intuition a bit, but that’s why I included an initial
> convergence window in the adaptation — we converge for a few iterations with a
> unit metric before beginning to learn a diagonal/dense one. If there are serious
> convergence issues it may very well be prescient to increase the size of this
> initial window.
>
> To summarize, convergence shouldn’t take much longer than optimization. Similarly,
> any “restarting distribution” will be fundamentally limited because by the time you’ve
> constructed a good one you already have enough information to construct your MCMC
> estimators. For example, if you want to initialize with EM then what initial conditions
> do you choose for the EM algorithm? You’re not solving the problem, just sweeping
> it under the rug of another step. Moreover, a good initialization or restarting distribution
> won’t be all that helpful for multimodal posteriors given that finding all of the modes
> will be incredibly difficult and even if you could find them all then you still have to be
> able to weight them appropriately in order to construct a valid MCMC transition
> (which means computing local evidences which means you need more than a
> simple Markov chain).
>

Cool..what a great discussion here!

@ Bob: Yes, your are right, I was suggesting an early stopping scheme. The idea is to a have cheap way to get close to the typical set - I do not care about the mode at all. All I want is to be close to the typical set (and somehow add noise coherent to some extent, the Fisher matrix sounds good, but is likely expensive to get ).

@ Michael: I am not sure if doing full blown MCMC is really so efficient here to find the starting points. You are right in that I would also need starting points for the more "simple minded" method, but I think that using a cheap method first should help in many instances to get a practical solution to the problem of getting sane inits.

@ Andrew: The graphical model thing sounds exciting and maybe this is a better approach to do these kind of things in a smart way as you have a lot more structural information at hand in that case.

In short: Complex models need clever initialization and if something smart can be done here, then this will be good for many, i.e. there are a number of users out there using very complex models to deal with their (complex) systems, but these users need good methods or guidance to handle those complex models the right way.

Sebastian
